## About {height=650px}

::: {.card .spacer width="25%"}
:::

::: {.card title="About this study" width="50%"}

I examined whether women and men are described differently in workplace feedback. Across several studies, I applied natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning to 2M+ feedback records from organisations on Culture Amp's platform.

**Methods**

- **Sentiment:** Classified how positive or negative feedback was, using a RoBERTa language model that agreed with human coders 89.9% of the time.
- **Emotions:** Identified 28 emotions, such as gratitude or admiration, using a language model trained on emotion-labelled text (GoEmotions).
- **Agentic and communal language:** Measured how close feedback was to agentic words (such as "ambitious") or communal words (such as "supportive"), using sentence embeddings.
- **Distinctive words:** Identified which words appeared more in feedback to women compared to men, using weighted log-odds.
- **Topics:** Identified the main themes in feedback by grouping words that often appear together (non-negative matrix factorisation, NMF).
- **Style:** Measured length, hedging, word variety and grammatical complexity.

**Data and privacy**

- Results are shown as aggregates only. No feedback texts or individual records are shared.

**Credits**

- PhD research at the [University of Melbourne](https://www.unimelb.edu.au/){target="_blank"}, in a research partnership with [Culture Amp](https://www.cultureamp.com/){target="_blank"}. Co-supervised by the University of Melbourne ([Computing and Information Systems](https://cis.unimelb.edu.au/){target="_blank"}) and [UC Berkeley Haas](https://haas.berkeley.edu/){target="_blank"}.
